issues.legal_issue: Land that becomes vacant land within an urban area after the commencement of the ceiling regime may be subjected to that regime from the date it acquires that status.
material_facts: The land was outside the urban limits when the ceiling regime commenced.
The land was brought within the urban area on a later date by an extension of the municipal limits.
The land was declared surplus and acquired after it entered the urban area.
issues.conclusion: The land could be subjected to the Act from the date it came within the municipal limits; the contrary rule in Atia Mohammadi Begum was not good law after N. Audikesava Reddy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1), including its explanation, and the definition of “master plan” in Section 2(h) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 contemplate land becoming vacant land after the Act commenced and require the relevant later master plan to be considered. State of A.P. v. N. Audikesava Reddy overruled the contrary view in Atia Mohammadi Begum v. State of U.P.

predicates.urban_land_ceiling_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether land is subject to an urban land ceiling regime.
predicates.land_entered_urban_scope_later: The land came within the legally defined urban scope after the regime commenced.

issues.definition: When an urban land ceiling proceeding concerns land that entered the regime’s urban scope later, the land is subject to the regime from the date it entered that scope.

issues.legal_issue: A valid acquisition followed by vesting of land in the State free from encumbrances cannot be undone by restoring the land to its former owner.
material_facts: The land was declared surplus and acquired under the ceiling regime.
The State took possession of the land and handed it over to a public corporation.
The former owner sought relief long after the acquisition.
issues.conclusion: Once the land vested in the State free from all encumbrances, it could not be divested, and the former owner was not entitled to restoration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(3) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, is analogous to Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Vesting free from encumbrances gives the State absolute title and possession and is not undone once possession has been taken. The Court relied on The Fruit & Vegetable Merchants Union v. Delhi Improvement Trust; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Tarsem Singh; Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P.; and the other authorities cited in paragraphs 8–12.

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns the acquisition of land by the State.
predicates.possession_taken: The State took possession of the land under the acquisition.

issues.definition: If a legally effective acquisition proceeding resulted in the State taking possession, the former owner is not entitled to restoration of the land.

issues.legal_issue: After land validly vests in the State free from encumbrances, the former owner cannot object to the State changing its use.
material_facts: The State acquired the land and took possession of it.
The State handed the land to a public corporation for a stated public purpose.
The public corporation used part of the land for a bus depot although the land had been earmarked for residential purposes.
issues.conclusion: The State could change the use of land after it vested in it, and the former owner could not challenge that change.
issues.legal_principle: Once land validly vests in the State free from encumbrances, its subsequent use is not a concern of the former owner, and a later diversion to another public purpose does not invalidate the acquisition. The Court relied on Gulam Mustafa v. State of Maharashtra; C. Padma v. Deputy Secretary to the Government of Tamil Nadu; Bhagat Singh v. State of U.P.; Niladri Narayan Chandradhurja v. State of West Bengal; and Northern Indian Glass Industries v. Jaswant Singh.

rule.if: acquisition_proceeding and valid_acquisition and possession_taken and state_changed_land_use

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns the acquisition of land by the State.
predicates.possession_taken: The State took possession of the land under the acquisition.
predicates.state_changed_land_use: After taking possession, the State or its transferee used the land for a purpose different from the one originally stated.

issues.definition: When the State validly acquires land, takes possession, and later changes its use, the former owner cannot challenge that changed use.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional power without a prescribed limitation period must be exercised within a reasonable time, and a substantially delayed challenge cannot unsettle final rights without adequate justification.
material_facts: The prescribed authority made a final order concerning the land, and an appeal route was available but not used.
The land was acquired and possession was taken many years before the revision was filed.
The revision was filed about two decades after the acquisition, without an adequate explanation for the delay.
The revisional authority allowed the revision without addressing the delay and relied on a decision that was later overruled.
issues.conclusion: The revisional authority could not use its power at this belated stage; the appeal was dismissed and the High Court’s decision setting aside the revision order stood.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, prescribes no limitation period, but that does not create an unlimited power: the power must be exercised within a reasonable time assessed in light of the facts and the nature of the order. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Patel Raghav Natha; Ibrahimpatnam Taluk Vyavasaya Coolie Sangham v. K. Suresh Reddy; State of A.P. v. T. Yadagiri Reddy; and the delay-and-laches authorities State of Karnataka v. S.M. Kotrayya, Jagdish Lal v. State of Haryana, and M/s. Rup Diamonds v. Union of India. A later decision granting relief to another person does not by itself explain the delay.

rule.if: statutory_revision_proceeding and no_fixed_time_limit and final_order_and_accrued_rights and substantial_unexplained_delay

predicates.statutory_revision_proceeding: The case concerns a statutory authority’s exercise of revisional power over an earlier order.
predicates.no_fixed_time_limit: The law authorising revision does not prescribe a specific time limit for exercising that power.
predicates.final_order_and_accrued_rights: The challenged order had attained finality and rights had accrued on its basis.
predicates.substantial_unexplained_delay: The revision was brought after a substantial period without an adequate explanation for the delay.

issues.definition: A revision brought after substantial unexplained delay cannot unsettle a final order and accrued rights merely because the law sets no specific time limit.

issues.legal_issue: Repeal of the ceiling regime does not entitle a former owner to recover land where the State had already taken possession.
material_facts: The land was acquired under the ceiling regime and possession was taken before the regime was repealed.
The former owner sought relief after the repeal.
issues.conclusion: The repeal did not confer any benefit on the former owner because possession had already been taken.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, pending proceedings abate where the tenure-holder remained in possession; repeal does not benefit the owner where possession was already taken. The Court relied on Pt. Madan Swaroop Shrotiya Public Charitable Trust v. State of U.P.; Ghasitey Lal Sahu v. Competent Authority; and Mukarram Ali Khan v. State of U.P.

predicates.urban_land_ceiling_proceeding: The case concerns proceedings under an urban land ceiling regime.
predicates.repeal_after_acquisition: The regime was repealed after the land had been acquired under it.
predicates.possession_taken_before_repeal: The State had taken possession before the repeal took effect.

issues.definition: When the regime is repealed after acquisition and the State had already taken possession, the former owner is not entitled to recover the land by reason of the repeal.
